summary.text: The Islamic Golden Age was a period of cultural flourishing in the history of Islam, dated from the 8th century to the 14th century.
It is understood to have begun under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid with the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, which drew scholars to translate classical knowledge into Arabic.
Learning also flourished in other cities such as Cairo and Umayyad Córdoba, and the period is said to have ended with the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

items.prompt: One 19th century author says the golden age ended after a few decades of early conquests, while another says it lasted for centuries. Why do they differ?

options.label: One of them had the wrong dates for the caliphate
One counted only Baghdad, the other counted Cairo as well
The term has no clear definition and depends on the focus
Scholars agreed to split the age into two eras

items.explain: There is no unambiguous definition, and depending on whether the focus is cultural or military achievement, the term may refer to quite different time spans.

items.prompt: Why do historians credit the translation work of this era with keeping ancient knowledge alive?

options.label: Many classic works that might have been lost were translated, some later into Hebrew and Latin
Scholars burned the originals so only the translations would remain
Only Greek works were copied, and they were never translated again
Translators wrote new works that replaced the older ones

items.explain: Many classic works of antiquity that might otherwise have been lost were translated from Greek, Syriac, Middle Persian, and Sanskrit into Syriac and Arabic, and some were later translated into Hebrew and Latin.

items.prompt: A top translator in Baghdad in the 800s is offered a salary. How well paid is he likely to be?

options.label: About the same as a labourer, since scholars worked for honour
Paid only in food and lodging at the palace
A modest stipend that rose only when he took students
A salary estimated to match those of professional athletes today

items.explain: The Islamic Empire heavily patronized scholars. The best scholars and notable translators, such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq, had salaries estimated to be equivalent to those of professional athletes today.

items.prompt: A bookseller in Samarkand is choosing between parchment, papyrus and paper. Which advantage of paper would he point to?

options.label: It was harder to produce, which kept books rare and valuable
It was easier to make than parchment and less likely to crack than papyrus
It took ink loosely, so notes could be wiped away and reused
It arrived from Europe and was already in wide use

items.explain: Paper was easier to manufacture than parchment, less likely to crack than papyrus, and absorbed ink so it was hard to erase. Paper spread into Muslim regions from China.

items.prompt: A newcomer claims the golden age was built by Arabic-speaking Muslims alone. Which fact corrects this?

options.label: Greek scholars were brought to Baghdad to run every institution
Christians were barred from scholarship by the Abbasids
Many House of Wisdom scholars were Christian, and many scientists were Persian
Almost all the scientists came from Baghdad itself

items.explain: Many scholars of the House of Wisdom were of Christian background and it was led by the Christian physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq. Persians also made up a notably high proportion of the scientists.

items.prompt: A scribe in Baghdad around 800 never calls his own age a "golden age". When did that label start being applied?

options.label: In the 19th century, in writing about Islamic history
During the reign of Harun al-Rashid, by his own court
Just after the Mongol siege of 1258, by those mourning it
During the Timurid Renaissance, to describe the earlier era

items.explain: The metaphor of a golden age began to be applied in 19th-century literature about Islamic history.

paragraphs.heading: A flowering of learning
paragraphs.text: The Islamic Golden Age was a time of cultural flowering in Islamic history, usually dated from the 8th to the 14th century. It is generally taken to start under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid (786–809), when the House of Wisdom was set up in Baghdad, then one of the largest cities in the world. This institution drew scholars from all over the Muslim world to put the classical learning of the known world into Arabic. Learning thrived beyond Baghdad too, in cities such as Cairo, Córdoba, Damascus, Samarkand and Fez, and later in Nasrid Granada.

paragraphs.heading: When did it end
paragraphs.text: Its end is usually placed in 1258, when the Mongols invaded, besieged Baghdad and brought down the Abbasid caliphate. Some scholars stretch it to about 1350 to take in the Timurid Renaissance. Others carry it into the 15th century to include the court of Granada, or even the 16th, with the rise of the Islamic gunpowder empires. There is no single agreed definition, and the span changes depending on whether the focus is culture or military success.

paragraphs.heading: Translating the ancients
paragraphs.text: The age is thought to have begun with a huge effort, in the eighth and ninth centuries, to gather and translate the ancient sciences of the Greeks. Muslims of the time were keen to absorb the scientific knowledge of the peoples they had conquered. Works by Galen, Hippocrates, Plato, Aristotle, Ptolemy and Archimedes were among those translated, out of Greek, Syriac, Middle Persian and Sanskrit and into Arabic and Syriac. Some of these texts, which might otherwise have been lost, were later passed on into Hebrew and Latin.

paragraphs.heading: Who did the work
paragraphs.text: Many translators were Christians, especially of the Church of the East, who turned Greek philosophy and science first into Syriac and then into Arabic. The House of Wisdom was led by the Christian physician Hunayn ibn Ishaq, and for a long time the caliphs' personal doctors were often Assyrian Christians, among them the Bukhtishu family. Persians also made up a notably large share of the scientists of the period. The empire backed scholars heavily, and top translators such as Hunayn are estimated to have earned what professional athletes earn today.

paragraphs.heading: Original science
paragraphs.text: After the translation era came two centuries of striking original thinking, lasting from the late ninth century to the late eleventh, often called the golden age of Islamic science. The period after it is conventionally known as the 'age of decline'. Since the nineteenth century, this story of decline has become the favoured framework in general scholarship.

paragraphs.heading: The power of paper
paragraphs.text: Paper reached Muslim lands from China in the eighth century, mass-produced in Samarkand and Khorasan, and arrived in Al-Andalus in the 10th century. It was easier to make than parchment, cracked less than papyrus, and soaked up ink so that writing was hard to rub out, which suited record-keeping. Islamic papermakers used assembly-line methods to copy manuscripts by hand, turning out editions larger than any in Europe for centuries. Together with a new, easier writing system, this meant that, probably for the first time, a person could live solely by writing and selling books.

paragraphs.heading: Faith and knowledge
paragraphs.text: Religion may have helped drive this search for knowledge. Quranic teachings that value education and stress learning may have pushed Muslims of the age to study and to build up science. The central place of scripture made education a pillar of Islam, and a saying attributed to Muhammad holds that seeking knowledge is a duty for every Muslim.
